title: How Netflix fits a 4 TB movie into 14 GB
description:
A 2-hour 4K movie, stored pixel by pixel (8.3 million pixels, 3 bytes each, 24 frames a second), is about 4.3 terabytes. Netflix streams 4K at up to 7 GB an hour, so about 14 GB: some 300 times smaller. Squeezing each frame like a JPEG gets you roughly 10x. The rest comes from between the frames: the picture is cut into blocks, and for most blocks the stream only says 'copy this block from the last frame, shifted a few pixels', plus the small leftover difference. A full picture is sent every couple of seconds so you can skip ahead. In one minute of Big Buck Bunny re-encoded with x264, a full picture took 130 KB and a predicted one about 8 KB: 16 times less.

Numbers checked in code (verify.py), including the x264 measurement on Big Buck Bunny (Blender Foundation, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons). Sources: Netflix Help Center (data usage), Wikipedia (Inter frame).

social_caption: A 4K movie is about 4 terabytes of pixels, and Netflix sends you 14 gigabytes. Here's the trick between the frames that makes up most of that.
facts_checked: Raw 4K: 3840 x 2160 = 8.29 million pixels x 3 bytes = 24.9 MB a frame; x 24 fps x 7,200 s = 4.3 TB; Netflix 2 h at 7 GB/h = 14 GB; ratio 307x; ~10x per-frame (JPEG, as measured in jpeg-tenth: 7-26x) -> ~430 GB, still ~31x too big (verify.py)
Netflix Ultra HD (4K): up to 7 GB per hour (https://help.netflix.com/en/node/87, fetched 2026-11-26)

Inter-frame coding: frame divided into macroblocks (16x16 in MPEG-2), motion vector points to the matching block in the reference frame, the prediction error is transformed and sent; I-frames decode on their own (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter_frame)

Measured: Big Buck Bunny 720p (Wikimedia Commons transcode), 1:00-2:00, x264 CRF 20, keyframe every 48 frames (2 s), no B-frames: keyframes average 130 KB, predicted frames 8.0 KB (16.3x less); 31 keyframes, 1,442 frames (verify.py)

beats.say: It's not a blurrier copy. It just never sends you the same thing twice.
Every frame is 8 million pixels, 3 bytes each, 24 frames a second. For 2 hours, that's your 4 terabytes.
beats.caption: Every frame is 8 million pixels, 3 bytes each, 24 frames a second. For 2 hours, that's your 4 TB.

beats.say: First, squeeze each frame like a JPEG. About 10 times smaller: 400 gigabytes.
beats.caption: First, squeeze each frame like a JPEG. About 10 times smaller: 400 GB.

beats.say: Still 30 times too big. The real trick is between the frames.
Two frames in a row are almost identical. So don't send frame 2. Send what changed.
Cut it into small blocks. For each one, send a single instruction: copy this block from the last frame, 3 pixels to the left. Plus the tiny difference left over.
Every 2 seconds, you still get one full picture: 130 kilobytes. The ones in between? About 8. Sixteen times less.
beats.caption: Every 2 seconds, you still get one full picture: 130 KB. The ones in between? About 8. 16 times less.

beats.say: That's how 4 terabytes become 14 gigabytes. 300 times smaller, and you never notice.
